## Proposal: cache for `GET /price`

The question isn't whether to cache. It's what to cache. We propose to cache the responses of `GET /price`, one entry per product ID.

It's not a CDN. It's not a second database. It's a read-through cache inside the pricing service. It runs in the existing pricing-service pods and needs no new servers.

The answer isn't more replicas. It's the cache.

It feels like a cache would serve stale prices. It's actually bounded: every entry expires after 30 seconds, and a price change deletes the entry for that product at once.

The cache is not just faster but also cheaper. In the load test, p99 latency of `GET /price` fell from 180 ms to 20 ms. The two extra replicas in the capacity plan would cost EUR 1,400 a month.

Requests that aren't in the cache are read from a database replica, and the cache skips any replica that isn't healthy.

The cache stops being useful when the hit rate drops below 60%, because most reads then still reach the database.

This design is about prices but not about discounts: `promo-svc` computes discounts, and this doc does not change it.

# Six months of running before work

From 6:10 to 6:50 nobody needs anything from me. I started running in that slot in April and have kept it up for six months.

The alarm isn't the problem. The shoes are. On the 19 mornings when I had to look for my shoes, I ran on only 4, though I woke up on time on all 19. Now I put them by the door the night before.

It wasn't the distance. It wasn't the pace. It was the routine.

Running slowly doesn't mean I'm lazy, but actually that I can keep going. At 7:30 per kilometre I can run 8 km; at 6:00 I stop after 3. It's not a race. It's my morning.

## Getting started

Installing `syncbox` is really simple. Just download the binary for your platform and put it on your `PATH`.

To start syncing a folder, simply run:

```sh
syncbox init ~/Documents --bucket s3://my-docs
```

`syncbox` actually builds the file index locally, so your file list never leaves your machine. Crucially, uploads run asynchronously: you can keep working while they finish.

Importantly, the first sync probably takes about an hour for 50 GB on a 100 Mbit/s connection. Later syncs upload only the files that changed.

Conflicts are inherently tricky. If the same file changed on two machines, `syncbox` keeps both copies and adds `.conflict` to the name of the older one.

Fundamentally, `syncbox` is a truly reliable tool, and you will inevitably come to depend on it.

# quarry 3.0

The search landscape is changing, and quarry 3.0 is a game-changer. In v3.0 we doubled down on indexing speed: a full reindex of the 40 GB benchmark corpus now takes 14 minutes instead of 52.

This is the deepest problem we have worked on. The old indexer wrote each segment twice. We took a step back, did a deep dive into the write path, and found that the second write only refreshed a checksum that the first write had already set.

Migrating an existing index is genuinely hard. v3 cannot read the v2 segment format, so you must reindex before you upgrade. The implications are significant. On a cluster, each node needs its own reindex. The stakes are high: an index that has not been reindexed stops answering queries after the upgrade. We'll unpack the reindex steps in the upgrade guide.

Moving forward, v2 gets security fixes until 2027-03-31. To navigate the upgrade, run `quarry reindex --dry-run`: it reports how long a reindex of your index will take.

In January I moved my to-do list from an app to a paper planner. The rest of this essay explains why, and what I lost.

You already know this, but apps are good at reminders. My old app sent me 14 reminders a day, and I ignored most of them. Plot twist: the planner sends none, and I get more done.

In this section, we'll look at the cost. As we'll see, it is search. To find a phone number I wrote down in January, I flip through 60 pages. Spoiler: I now put phone numbers in my contacts app instead (yes, I see the irony).
